title: Who does what: the roles working together
blurb: Bring all seven roles together: who owns what, who decides what, how problems escalate, and how to separate the pairs the exam loves to confuse.
question: A developer on a school's new learning platform finds a problem that will delay launch beyond the agreed tolerance. Trace what happens next: who logs it, who decides, who supports, and who tests the revised release?

teach.body: Every project role answers three questions: what do they own, what can they decide, and what do they do? One person, the sponsor, is accountable: they answer for the project meeting its need and delivering benefits. Many people are responsible for parts of it: the project manager for day-to-day delivery, the team for the work, the product owner for the backlog. The PMO supports them all, and the governance board directs.

root.label: Governance board
root.sub: chaired by the sponsor; senior user and supplier reps

teach.caption: On iterative work, a product owner works with the team, representing users and owning the backlog.
Inside tolerance, the project manager resolves the problem and reports it. Only problems beyond tolerance become issues for the sponsor.

teach.body: At Elm Park School, a developer (team member) finds the platform won't link to the pupil database without extra work. She tells the project manager, who forecasts a five-week delay against a three-week tolerance and escalates it. The deputy head (sponsor) takes it to the board, where a teacher sits as senior user. They drop the parent-chat feature through change control. The PMO updates its report; teachers (end users) test the revised release.

Whether the outputs meet users' needs
Which risk register template to use

teach.text: Read the verb in the option. Owns the business case, secures funding, approves, chairs, champions: SPONSOR. Plans, manages, maintains, reports, escalates: PROJECT MANAGER. Directs and decides at gates: BOARD. Prioritises the backlog: PRODUCT OWNER. Provides, supports, assures: PMO. Delivers work packages: TEAM. Uses, accepts, adopts: END USERS.

items: One accountable sponsor; many people responsible for parts of the work.
The PM resolves problems within tolerance; issues beyond it are escalated to the sponsor, who (with the board) agrees the resolution.
Sponsor owns the business case; PM owns the PMP; product owner owns the backlog; team delivers work packages.
The board directs and decides; the PMO supports and assures; end users accept and adopt the outputs.

summary: You can now match every PFQ role to what it owns, decides and does, follow a problem from discovery to resolution through the correct roles, and separate the most-confused pairs, especially the sponsor and the project manager.

A.q: Which role is accountable, rather than simply responsible, for a project meeting its identified need?
A.why: The sponsor is the single senior individual accountable for the work being governed effectively and meeting the identified need.

whyNot.1: The project manager is responsible for day-to-day delivery, under the sponsor's accountability.
whyNot.2: The team is responsible for its work packages, not accountable for the whole project.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports projects and is not accountable for any of them.

A.q: Which pairing of role and document is correct?
A.why: The sponsor owns the business case.

whyNot.0: The product backlog is owned by the product owner.
whyNot.1: The PMO supports projects; it does not own business cases.
whyNot.3: The project manager owns the project management plan; the team works to it.

A.q: A team member reports a problem the project manager can fix without breaching any tolerance. Who should resolve it?
A.why: Problems within delegated tolerance are resolved by the project manager, who then reports them; they are not issues for the sponsor.

whyNot.0: The sponsor deals with issues escalated beyond tolerance, not routine problems.
whyNot.2: The board makes key decisions; it does not need to resolve problems within the PM's authority.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports and reports; it does not manage the project's problems.

B.q:
Which TWO decisions would normally be taken above the project manager?
1) Accepting a forecast cost overrun beyond tolerance
2) Re-ordering two tasks that have float
3) Whether to continue past a decision gate
4) Choosing a time for the weekly team meeting
B.why: A cost overrun beyond tolerance (1) is an issue for the sponsor, and gate decisions (3) belong to the sponsor or board.

whyNot.0: Re-ordering tasks with float (2) is within the project manager's authority.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 4 are routine project manager decisions.
whyNot.2: Setting a meeting time (4) is a routine project manager decision.

B.q: What is the key difference between a PMO and a project manager?
options: PMO supports many; PM manages one
PMO manages one; PM supports many
PMO owns benefits; PM the business case
PMO accepts outputs; PM sets strategy
B.why: A PMO provides support across projects, while a project manager manages the day-to-day delivery of one project.

whyNot.2: Benefits and the business case both belong to the sponsor.
whyNot.3: End users accept outputs, and strategy is set at organisational level.

B.q: What is the key difference between the governance board and the PMO?
options: The PMO decides; the board advises
They share every gate decision equally
The board decides; the PMO supports
The board runs the project daily
B.why: The board gives direction and makes key decisions; the PMO supports governance with reporting and assurance but does not decide.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two: decisions sit with the board.
whyNot.1: Gate decisions are taken by the sponsor or board, not shared with the PMO.
whyNot.3: Daily running of the project is the project manager's job, not the board's.

C.q: On a theatre refurbishment, a site team member spots a delay that will push opening night beyond the time tolerance. Which route should the problem take?
C.why: The team member raises it with the project manager, who assesses it and, because it breaches tolerance, escalates it to the sponsor.

whyNot.0: This runs backwards: problems are escalated upwards, not handed down.
whyNot.2: The PMO and end users are not the escalation route for a delivery problem.
whyNot.3: The problem starts with the team member, and the PM escalates to the sponsor, who may involve the board.

C.q: Which statement about the sponsor and the project manager is correct?
options: The sponsor writes the plan; the PM approves it
Both jointly own the business case equally
The PM owns benefits; the sponsor the outputs
The PM writes the plan; the sponsor approves it
C.why: The project manager writes, owns and maintains the project management plan; the sponsor approves it.

whyNot.1: The sponsor alone owns the business case; the PM contributes to it.
whyNot.2: The sponsor is accountable for benefits; the PM is responsible for delivering outputs.

C.q: Which role is matched with the WRONG responsibility?
C.why: Gate decisions are taken by the sponsor or governance board. The PMO may support the gate review but does not decide.

whyNot.1: Securing funding is correctly matched to the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Reporting progress is correctly matched to the project manager.
whyNot.3: Prioritising the backlog is correctly matched to the product owner.

reteach.title: Everyone at the wedding has a job
reteach.question: Picture a wedding: the couple paying, a family committee, a wedding planner, the caterers and florists, the venue's events office and the guests. Which project role is each?

blocks.body: The couple are the sponsor: they want it, pay for it and judge whether it was worth it. The family committee they chair is the governance board. The planner is the project manager. Caterers and florists are team members doing the work. The venue's events office is like a PMO: it supplies checklists and timings but runs nobody's wedding. The guests are the end users: the day has to work for them.

blocks.text: If the caterer is going to be late, the planner sorts it. If the venue burns down, the couple decide. Within tolerance: project manager. Beyond it: sponsor.

explain.body: Sponsor: business case and benefits. Project manager: the project management plan. Product owner: the backlog. Team: their work packages. PMO: standards and templates.

test.q: Which list gives the owners of the business case, the project management plan and the product backlog, in that order?
test.why: The sponsor owns the business case, the project manager owns the project management plan and the product owner owns the backlog.

whyNot.0: The first two are swapped: the sponsor owns the business case.
whyNot.1: The PM owns the plan and the product owner owns the backlog, not the other way round.

explain.body: The governance board, chaired by the sponsor, directs and decides. The project manager manages within the limits set. The team delivers the work. The PMO supports all of them.

test.q: Which statement about authority on a project is correct?
options: The PM directs, the board manages, the team delivers
The board directs, the PM manages, the team delivers
The team directs, the PM delivers, the board manages
The PMO directs, the sponsor delivers, the PM manages
test.why: The board directs, the project manager manages day to day and the team delivers the work.

whyNot.0: The board directs; the PM manages.
whyNot.2: The team does not direct the project.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports rather than directs, and the sponsor does not deliver the work.

explain.body: Inside tolerance the project manager resolves problems and reports them. A problem that breaches, or is about to breach, tolerance is an issue: it is escalated to the sponsor, who agrees the resolution.

test.q: In APM terms, an issue is a problem that…
options: may arise in future and is uncertain
the PM can fix within the current plan
the team has resolved and closed
test.why: An issue is a problem that is breaching, or about to breach, the delegated tolerances and needs the sponsor's support to resolve.

whyNot.0: An uncertain future event is a risk, not an issue.
whyNot.1: Problems the PM can fix within tolerance are not issues in the APM sense.
whyNot.2: A resolved and closed problem is no longer a live issue.

explain.body: The sponsor is accountable: owns the business case, secures funding, approves the plan, chairs the board. The project manager is responsible: writes the plan, runs delivery, reports and escalates.

test.q: Which pair of words best separates the sponsor's position from the project manager's?
test.why: The sponsor is accountable for the project as a whole; the project manager is responsible for managing its delivery.

whyNot.1: Informed and consulted describe stakeholders who are kept updated or asked for views, not these two roles.
whyNot.2: Neither role is defined by technical or financial expertise.
whyNot.3: Both roles are closely involved in the project; neither is defined as independent of it.
